Well, for starters, it would be great if we knew which article you were referring to, so we could tell you whether or not we agree with the points listed in the article in question.

That being said, as someone who regularly does PC Repair and custom builds for his clients, I recommend each OS/Hardware Model on a case-by-case basis, depending on what the client's needs are. Think of it like a car. The guy who is hauling around a family of 5 isn't going to be too interested in a Lamborghini for the family car...he's going to be much more interested in a Mercury Sable or a Ford Explorer...maybe an F150 Pickup, if he wants to be able to haul things. Meanwhile, the engine hobbyist is going to say "Fuck all that noise" and just get himself a Kit Car.

It's much the same way with computers. For those who want simplicity, first and foremost, and don't want to get "Under the hood", so to speak, in understanding the inner workings of their computer, I recommend Mac, because it's a canned user experience that basically just does what its user wants it to. Want to browse YouTube? Just start up the YouTube App. Browse the Web? Start up the Browser App. User Experience in a Can...just don't expect to go much outside that walled garden. It's convenient, but you pay a price for that convenience, hence higher retail price for simplicity and Status-brand recognition.

If the User is willing to learn some basic Tech Knowhow, I go the route of suggesting Windows. Gives a bit more freedom, and has the added plus of not being tied down to a proprietary hardware format. Lots of part competitors means lots of cheap parts for upgrading, in the future. Requires a bit more work, but if the User is willing to teach themself what they need to know...not my issue.

Finally, for hobbyists, I recommend one of several Linux distros. These are usually the people who know what they're doing when they crack open a case, and either have experience writing custom firmware, or have the knowhow to track down a tutorial on how to do so.

Final Verdict: "Superior" is subjective, and dependent upon what the needs of the User are. A User that requires the ability to upgrade his box on-the-fly is going to think that Mac's proprietary hardware model is absolute shit, while a User that doesn't want to deal with that mess will find it superior. Figure out the User's needs, and tailor your recommendations accordingly. And in full disclosure, I say this as someone who dual-boots Windows7 and Mint Linux, with an absolute revulsion and personal hatred for anything Apple-related. In the end, it's all about satisfying the needs of the User...my personal opinions of the brands has little in relevance to that topic.

It depends on how much you're willing to spend and what you want to do with the computer. If you're a gamer, then PC. Not that there aren't AAA titles on OSX, but the games library doesn't compare to what you'll get on a PC. You'll spend more on a Mac, and will probably have fewer upgrade options as a lot of Macs today just aren't easily serviceable by the average Joe and in most cases, are completely non-upgradable, especially the recent iterations of the Mac Mini. Whatever configuration you initially go with is soldered directly to the logic board. So if you buy a system with 8 GB of RAM (bare minimum for current versions of OSX) and lower end SSD drive, you're stuck with that config until you buy a new system. The MacBook Pro line should still be upgradeable in terms of memory and possibly HD/SSD, but I'm not sure. The MacBook line is probably all soldered down and in reality, you're better off getting a MacBook Air as it has a faster processor, more ports and a standard MagSafe adapter. The Mac Pro line is ridiculously overpriced and out of date tech wise so I wouldn't even look at that as an option. And the iMac line is so thin that it's almost impossible to work on if it's even upgradable at all (a la the Mini).

If you're wanting a small, solid, lightweight (in terms of actual weight) machine to surf the web, do email, run some games, maybe even do some development work on, the MacBook Air is probably your best bet. You can install Windows on it either through a virtual machine like VMware or VirtualBox, or use Apple's Bootcamp software to install Windows on it's own partition. The advantage to the former is that you can run both OS's simultaneously albeit with some limitations (Windows won't perform as well as if it was running natively). The advantage to the latter is that Windows will run just as it would on a PC except you'll have to specifically reboot into it each time. Macs are also inherently more secure as it doesn't give you super user or root privileges right out of the box the way that Windows does. Even though you're account will be admin class, you'll need to type your password to make any major system changes which IMHO is a good thing as you won't just be blindly clicking 'Yes/OK/Continue' and accidentally install something you don't want. Software only has as much privileges as the user sitting at the keyboard. Not to say there isn't malware on Macs, just that it's more difficult for it to get a foothold because of Unix/BSD nature of the underlying system.

On the PC side, you can run just about anything. You could put together a smoking system for a price somewhere between a Mini and one of Apples low end laptops and 'Hackintosh' it. It's a bit complicated to do but possible. So you could theoretically dualboot between Windows and OSX, and probably even Linux. Lot's more options on the PC side for a lower price.
